paragraphs.text: And God planted a paradise in Eden toward the east, and there he placed the man whom he had formed.

As we set out to speak about paradise, we feel no small anxiety in wanting to inquire into and explain what paradise is, where it is, and what it is like. This is all the more so because the Apostle does not know whether he was in the body or out of the body, yet says he was caught up to the third heaven. And again he says: "I know such a man—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows—that he was caught up into paradise and heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter. Of such a one I will boast, but of myself [?] I will not boast, except in my weaknesses. For if I wish to boast, I shall not be a fool, for I speak the truth." So if paradise is such that only Paul, or scarcely anyone like Paul, could see it while still living in this life, and yet even he could not remember whether he saw it in the body or out of the body, though he heard words that he was forbidden to make known, how then shall we be able to settle the location of paradise, which we have not been able to see, and which, even if we had been able to see it, we would still be forbidden to make known to others? At the same time, since Paul was afraid of being exalted by the loftiness of his revelations, how much more must we take care not to disclose too eagerly something whose very revelation is exposed to danger! We ought not, then, to think this paradise a common thing, and so let us leave it as Paul's secret.

Yet since we read in Genesis that paradise was planted by God toward the east, and that the man whom God had formed was placed there, we can at least discover who made this paradise. For who could have fashioned paradise but almighty God, who spoke and things were made, and who never lacked anything he wished to bring into being? He himself, then, planted paradise, of which Wisdom says: "Every plant that my Father has not planted shall be rooted up." Good is the planting of the angels, good that of the saints; for the saints are said to dwell under the fig tree and the vine in that future time of peace, and in these trees there is a figure of the angels.

Paradise, then, has many trees, but fruit-bearing trees, trees full of sap and vigor, of which it is said: "All the trees of the forest shall rejoice"—trees always flowering with the green of their merits, like that tree which is planted by the streams of water, whose leaf shall not fall, because in it all fruit abounds. This, then, is paradise.

The place where it was planted is called Delight. So holy David says: "You shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight." For you have read that a spring comes forth from Eden which waters paradise. These trees, then, which are planted in paradise, are watered as if by the flowing of a torrent of the Spirit. Of this he also says elsewhere: "The rush of the river makes glad the city of God." And that city is the Jerusalem above, which is free, in which the varied merits of the saints have sprung up.

In this paradise, then, God placed the man whom he had formed. Understand, then, that he did not place there the man who is according to the image of God, but the man who is according to the body; for what is incorporeal is not in a place. He placed him in paradise as he placed the sun in the sky, waiting for the kingdom of heaven, just as creation waits for the revelation of the sons of God.

If, then, paradise is where the shrubs had sprung up, paradise seems to be the soul, which multiplies the seed it has received, in which each virtue is planted, and in which there was also the tree of life, that is, wisdom. As Solomon said, wisdom did not spring from the earth but from the Father; for she is the radiance of eternal light and an outflowing of the glory of the Almighty.

There was also the tree of the knowledge of good and evil in paradise. For so you read: God brought forth a tree beautiful to the eye and good for food, and the tree of life in paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Later we shall see whether this tree too was beautiful to the eye and good for food like the others. That question will be discussed more fittingly at the point where we find that the man who tasted of it was deceived. For the present we have nothing we ought to find fault with, even if we cannot know the reason. For neither in this created world, if some things seem hard for us to understand and beyond the grasp of our minds, ought we to condemn them by some rash judgment—as for instance the creation of serpents or of some venomous animal—since we human beings are not yet able to understand and know for what reason each particular thing was made. So too in the divine Scriptures, let us not readily find fault with anything we cannot understand; for there are very many things that are not to be measured by our minds, but are to be judged from the depth of the divine plan and Word.

Suppose—without prejudice, however, to what will be argued later—that this tree of the knowledge of good and evil displeases you because, after people tasted of it, they realized that they were naked. Even so, I will tell you that, for the completion of God's work, this tree too sprang up in paradise and was permitted by God so that we might be able to know the surpassing excellence of the good. For if there were no knowledge of good and evil, how would we learn any distinction between good and evil? We would not judge what was evil to be evil unless there were knowledge of the good—and there could be no knowledge of the good unless the good also existed—nor again would we know that what was good was good unless there were knowledge of evil. Take an example from the very constitution of the human body. It certainly contains a certain bitterness of gall, which, if you look at the body as a whole, is found to be useful for a person's health. So too what we think evil is often not evil in every respect, but useful for the whole. For just as the gall is in one part of the body and yet serves the good of the whole body, so God, knowing that the knowledge of good and evil would serve the good of all, established it in a part, so that it might benefit the whole.

Then again, you find the serpent in paradise, certainly not brought into being without God's will. In the figure of the serpent is the devil; for the prophet Ezekiel also teaches that the devil was in paradise, when he says of the prince of Tyre: "You were made in the delight of paradise"; and we take the prince of Tyre as a figure of the devil. Shall we accuse God on this account too, because we cannot grasp the treasures of his depth and knowledge, hidden and concealed in Christ, except those he himself has deigned to reveal? Yet he has revealed this much, so that we may know that even the devil's malice serves the salvation of human beings—not because the devil wants to help, but because the Lord turns his malice, resisting though he is, to our salvation. Thus his malice made the virtue and patience of the holy man Job shine more brightly. His malice exercised Job's righteousness, so that he might contend and conquer, and a crown might follow the victory; for no one is crowned unless he has contended lawfully. Joseph's chastity, too, would never have come down to our memory had not his master's wife, stirred by the fiery darts of the devil, tempted his affections, and had she not at last sought his death, so that the chastity of the man who despised death for the sake of chastity might shine the more. Do you wish to know God's plan? Certainly it seems that, at the devil's instigation, death is prepared for righteous men, and even the murder of sons is carried out. Yet the Lord tested Abraham by this very means, asking him to sacrifice his son to him. By this test Abraham was proved faithful to the Lord, since not even pity for his beloved son drew him back from the obedience of his devotion. So also the tree of the knowledge of good and evil in paradise, which was beautiful to the sight and good for food, seemed so in appearance; for it was not good for food in its use, since eating of it is seen to have harmed human beings. So there is something that harms individuals but benefits the whole. Thus the devil harmed Judas, but apart from him he brought crowns to all the apostles, who overcame the temptations of his malice.

We should therefore neither doubt nor find fault with the fact that the devil was in paradise, since he could not shut off the way to the saints so that none might ascend; nor did he, as though he were its owner, snatch away from the righteous their dwelling place. Granted that he turned some idle and vicious people away from dwelling in the heavenly possession: it is far more glorious and far more beautiful that he will be shut out by the prayers of the saints, when that word is fulfilled: "I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven." So let us not fear him, who is so weak that he himself is to fall to the earth. He did indeed receive leave to tempt, but he did not receive power to overthrow, unless a weak will slips of its own accord, not knowing how to call for help. And therefore we need to learn by what deceit he tempted the first man, what in man he thought should be tempted, in what order and by what art, so that we may be on our guard.

Many, however, who hold that the devil was not in paradise—although we have read that he stood in heaven with the angels—may, so as not to seem offended by this account, take the interpretation of this passage according to their own preference. For before us there was one who said that the transgression was committed by man through pleasure and sense: he took the figure of the serpent to represent delight, and in the figure of the woman he placed the sense-perception of the soul and mind, which the Greeks call aisthēsis; and he declared that, once sense had been deceived, the mind, which the Greeks call nous, became the transgressor, according to the story. Rightly, then, in Greek nous is taken as the figure of the man and aisthēsis as that of the woman. Hence some have also interpreted Adam as earthly nous. And the Lord in the Gospel set forth those virgins awaiting the bridegroom's coming with lamps lit or extinguished to represent the senses, whether sound in the wise or corrupted in the foolish. For if Eve, that is, the sense of the first woman, had kept her lamps lit, she would never have entangled us in the snares of her transgression, nor would she have fallen from that immortality of virtue.

Paradise, then, is a kind of fertile land, that is, a fruitful soul, planted in Eden, that is, in a certain delight, or in well-tilled ground, in which the soul may find delight. There is also nous, as Adam, and there is sense, as Eve. And so that you would have nothing to blame on the weakness of nature or on a condition vulnerable in the face of dangers, consider what aids this soul has.

There was a spring that watered paradise. What spring is this but the Lord Jesus Christ, the spring of eternal life, as is the Father? For it is written: "For with you is the fountain of life," and again: "Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water." Both a spring is spoken of and a river, which waters the fruitful tree of paradise so that it bears fruit unto eternal life. This, then, is the spring, as you have read—for it says, "A spring comes forth from Eden," that is, there is a spring in your soul, whence Solomon too says: "Drink water from your own vessels and from the springs of your own wells"—this is the spring that comes forth from that well-tilled soul full of delight, this the spring that waters paradise, that is, the virtues of the soul, sprouting with the highest merit.

"And the spring," it says, "is divided into four heads. The name of the first is Pishon; this is the one that flows around the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold. And the gold of that land is good, and there is the carbuncle and the green stone. And the name of the second is Gihon; this is the one that flows around the whole of Ethiopia. And the third river is the Tigris; this is the one that flows toward the Assyrians. And the fourth river is the Euphrates." These, then, are the four rivers: namely the Pishon—called Pishon by the Hebrews, but Ganges by the Greeks—which flows toward India; the Gihon, which is the Nile, flowing around the land of Egypt or Ethiopia; and Mesopotamia is so called because the Tigris and Euphrates enclose it, since it lies between these two rivers, as the very name and common opinion have made known even to those living far away. But how is the wisdom of God called a spring? It is a spring according to the Gospel, which says: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink"; and it is a spring according to the prophet, who says: "Come, eat of my bread and drink the wine I have mixed for you." Just as wisdom, then, is the spring of life, the spring of spiritual grace, so it is the spring of the other virtues, which direct us on the course toward eternal life. It is from this soul, then, the cultivated one, not from the uncultivated, that this spring comes forth to water paradise, that is, a kind of thicket of the various virtues, which have four heads into which this wisdom is divided. What are the four heads of the virtues but, first, prudence; second, temperance; third, fortitude; fourth, justice? These the wise men of this world also borrowed from us and carried over into the writings of their books. And so, just as wisdom is the spring, these four rivers are streams of the virtues flowing from that spring.

Pishon, then, is prudence, and therefore it has good gold, the shining carbuncle, and the green stone. For we often take gold to stand for the discoveries of the prudent; hence the Lord also says through the prophet: "I gave them gold and silver"; and David says of the prudent: "If you sleep among the lots, the wings of a dove covered with silver, and her hinder parts with the sheen of gold"—meaning that one who has held fast to the Old and New Testaments can advance, through the richness of discourse, into the very secrets of God's wisdom. This, then, we may call good gold, not the gold of coinage, which is corruptible and earthly. It also has, it says, the shining carbuncle, in which a certain little spark of our soul lives. And it has the green stone, which by the appearance of its color seems to display something fresh and full of life. For shrubs that live are green, while whatever dies withers; the earth is green while it blooms, and seeds are green as they burst forth. And rightly is this river, Pishon, put in first place, which among the Hebrews is called Pheison, that is, "change of mouth" [?], since it flows around not just one nation but also flows through Lydia. For prudence is not something narrow, but rich in benefits, profitable to many. It comes first so that, if anyone has gone out of paradise, the river of prudence, as it were, may receive him, so that he may not quickly wither, but may through it easily return to paradise. This river is frequented by many people and is said to have very great beauty and fertility. And therefore prudence is understood under its figure, which bore abundant fruit at the coming of the saving Lord. It also flows to the ends of the earth, because all people have been redeemed through wisdom. Hence it is said: "Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world."

The second river is the Gihon, near which the law was given to the Israelites while they were settled in Egypt: that they should depart from Egypt and, with their loins girded, eat the lamb—which is a mark of temperance, for the Lord's Passover must be celebrated by those who are chaste and sanctified. And so it was near this river that the observance of the law was first established, because this name signifies a kind of chasm in the earth. For just as a chasm swallows up earth and whatever refuse or filth is in it, so chastity is accustomed to do away with all the passions of the body; and fittingly the observance was first established there, because through the law the sin of the flesh is swallowed up. Rightly, then, is the Gihon, which is a figure of chastity, said to flow around the land of Ethiopia, so as to wash the lowly body and quench the fire of the most base flesh; for Ethiopia, translated into Latin, signifies "lowly" and "base." And what is more lowly than our body, what so like Ethiopia, since it too is black with a kind of darkness of sins?

The third river is the Tigris, which flows toward the Assyrians, to whom transgressing Israel was led captive. This river is said to be swifter than all the others, and the Assyrians dwell by it, that is, "those who direct," for this is what the name means. So whoever by fortitude of soul has taken captive the transgressing vices of the body, directing himself toward things above, is reckoned like this river. And so fortitude too flows from that spring which is in paradise. Fortitude, with a kind of rapid course, strikes through whatever stands in its way, and its course is not held back by any obstacles.

The fourth river is the Euphrates, whose name in Latin means fruitfulness and abundance of produce, displaying a mark of justice, which nourishes every soul. For no virtue seems to bear more abundant fruit than equity and justice, which benefits others more than itself and neglects its own advantage, putting the common good first. Many think the Euphrates is named apo tou euphrainesthai, that is, from rejoicing, because the human race rejoices in nothing more than in justice and equity. As for why the regions through which the other rivers pass are described, while the regions through which the Euphrates passes are not, we take the reason to be this: its water is said to be life-giving and to nourish and increase; hence the learned among the Hebrews and Assyrians called it Auxen, whereas the water of the other rivers is said to be the opposite. Moreover, where there is prudence there is also cunning, where there is fortitude there is wrath, where there is temperance there is often intemperance and other vices; but where there is justice there is the harmony of all the other virtues. So it is not known from the places through which it flows, that is, not from a part; for justice is not a part, but as it were the mother of all. In these four rivers, then, the four principal virtues are expressed, which have, as it were, enclosed the ages of this world.

The first age, then, from the beginning of the world until the Flood, was the age of prudence. In this age are counted the righteous: Abel, so called by the Lord [?]; and Enosh, that is, man made in the image of God, who hoped to call on the name of the Lord God; and Enoch, whose name in Latin means "grace of God," who was caught up to heaven; and Noah, who was himself both just and a kind of guiding toward rest.

The second age is that of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and the rest of the number of the patriarchs, in whom a chaste and pure temperance of religion shone forth. For Isaac was spotless, a son given to Abraham through the promise, displaying not so much a bodily birth as the gift of divine favor; in him a figure of the truly Spotless One went before, as the Apostle teaches when he says that the promises were made to Abraham and to his seed. He does not say, "and to seeds," as of many, but as of one, "and to your seed," who is Christ.

The third age is in the law of Moses and the other prophets. For time will fail me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, [Solomon,] David and Samuel and the other prophets, Ananias, Azarias, Misael, Daniel, Elijah, Elisha, who through faith conquered kingdoms, wrought justice, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, grew strong out of weakness, became mighty in war, and took the camps of foreigners. Not without reason, then, is the figure of fortitude found in them. For they were sawn asunder, as you read further on, they were tempted, they died by the slaughter of the sword. They went about in goatskins, destitute, afflicted, and tormented with pains, men of whose merits the world was not worthy, wandering in deserts, in mountains, in caves, and in holes of the earth. Rightly, then, do we place the figure of fortitude in them.

The age according to the Gospel is a worthy figure of justice, because it is the power unto salvation for everyone who believes. Indeed, the Lord himself says: "Permit us to fulfill all justice." Justice is the fruitful parent of the other virtues, although in whomever one of those virtues we have named is principal, the others too are present in him, because the virtues are bound together and joined with one another. For certainly Abel was just, Abraham most brave and most patient, the prophets most prudent; and Moses, learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, esteemed the reproach of Christ a greater honor than the treasures of Egypt. And who was wiser than Daniel? Solomon too asked for wisdom and was granted it. So much, then, for the four rivers of the virtues, whose drink is beneficial. And since Pishon was said to have the good gold of the land, and the carbuncle, and the green stone, let us consider also what this means.

Enosh, who prudently desired to know the name of God, seems to us like good gold. Enoch, who was translated and did not see death, is a kind of carbuncle, a sweet-smelling stone, which holy Enoch offered to God by his works, breathing forth a certain grace in his deeds and character. Noah, like the green stone, displayed the color of life, since at the time of the Flood he alone was preserved in that ark as a living seed, so to speak, for the order of things to come. Rightly, then, is paradise, which is watered by many rivers, toward the east, not against the east—that is, toward that East whose name is the Dayspring, namely toward Christ, who poured forth a radiance of eternal light—and it is in Eden, that is, in delight.

: And God took the man whom he had made and placed him in paradise to work it and to guard it. You see that one who already existed is taken up; and he was in the land where he had been formed. So the power of God took hold of him, breathing into him progress and growth in virtue. Then he placed him in paradise, so that you may know that being taken up meant being breathed upon, as it were, by divine power. Notice here that the man was made outside paradise and the woman inside paradise, so that you may see that each person wins grace for himself not by the nobility of place or of birth but by virtue. In fact the man, who was made outside paradise, that is, in an inferior place, proves to be the better, while she who was made in the better place, that is, in paradise, is found to be the inferior; for the woman was deceived first, and she herself deceived the man. Hence the apostle Peter recalled that holy women, subject to the stronger vessel, obeyed their husbands as lords. And Paul says that Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and fell into transgression. Next we must observe that no one ought readily to presume on himself. For see: she who was made to be a help to the man needs a man's protection, because the man is the head of the woman; while he who believed he would have his wife's help fell through his wife. Therefore no one should readily entrust himself to another unless he has proved that person's virtue; nor should one who thinks he has been taken on as a helper claim anything for himself. Rather, if he finds that the one he thought he was protecting is the stronger, let him borrow grace from that person, just as the apostle Peter instructs husbands to show honor to their wives, saying: Husbands, likewise, live with your wives with understanding, showing honor to the woman as to the weaker vessel, as to fellow heirs of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered.

So the man was placed in paradise, and the woman was made in paradise; but even then, before the woman was deceived by the serpent, she had the grace of the man, since she was taken from the man—though this is a great mystery, as the apostle said—and therefore she drew the source of her life from him. And so Scripture said of the man alone that God placed him in paradise to work it and to guard it. To work and to guard are not the same. In working there is a certain progress in virtue; in guarding one discerns a certain completion of the work, since one guards things that are, so to speak, already completed. These two things are required of man: that he should seek new things by his works and guard what he has gained. This is the general meaning. Philo, however, since with his Jewish disposition he did not grasp spiritual things, kept to the moral sense, saying that these two things are required: work in the field and the guarding of the house. And although paradise, he says, had no need of farm work, still, because the first man was to be the law for his descendants, he took on even in paradise the form of lawful labor, in order to bind us to the work and guarding of the duty we owe and to the obligation of hereditary succession. These two things, then, are demanded of you, whether in the moral or the spiritual sense. The prophetic psalm also teaches you this, for it is written: Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain; unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it have kept watch in vain. You see that those labor who are in the process of working and building, while those keep watch who have already taken over the guarding of a finished work. Hence the Lord also said to the apostles, as to those already more perfect: Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation. He was teaching that the gift of a perfected nature and the grace of full virtue must be preserved, and that no one, however perfect, ought to feel secure about himself unless he keeps watch.

And the Lord God commanded Adam, saying: From every tree that is in paradise you shall eat for food, but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat; for on the day you eat of it you shall die the death. Why, when he commanded that they eat from every tree, did he say in the singular, "you shall eat," but concerning the tree of the knowledge of good and evil said in the plural, "you [all] shall not eat"? It is no idle question. But if you look carefully, it can be resolved by the authority of the Scriptures. For what is good is also to be done; and what is good and to be done is harmonious and cohesive, whereas what is shameful is discordant, disordered and divided. And therefore the Lord, who always aims at unity, gave his command in terms of unity. Indeed, he who made both one works unity; and not only both, but he made all one, for he bade us all be one body and one spirit. And through all things the firstborn, since he is in unity with the Father, is always most closely joined to the Father, because the Word was with God. Accordingly he says: I and the Father are one, to show that he has unity of majesty and divinity with the Father. But he also commanded us to be one, and poured into us, through the grace of adoption, a likeness of his own nature and unity, saying: Father, as you and I are one, so may these also be one in us. So when he commands what is good, he commands as though addressing one, saying, "you shall eat"; for unity cannot transgress. But when he says that the tree of the knowledge of good and evil must not be tasted, he speaks as though to many, "you shall not eat"; for what is a prohibition is enjoined as upon many. I, however, think something else, and I find already in God's very words what was to happen. He commanded Adam alone to taste of every tree, since he knew Adam would keep the command; but concerning not tasting the tree of the knowledge of good and evil he speaks no longer in the singular but in the plural. For he knew that the woman would transgress, and so by the plural he shows that they would not keep it, since the judgment of many is divided.

As far as the version of the Seventy is concerned, then, the difficulty has been resolved. But since Symmachus put both in the singular, we understand that he followed the practice whereby in the law, too, when God addresses the people, he speaks in the singular, as you have: Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one Lord; and, You shall love the Lord your God. Nor does the interpretation of Symmachus prejudice my view, for he could not see the unity of the Father and the Son, even though both Aquila and he himself have sometimes acknowledged it in their wording. And let no one think that what we said above is contradicted by the fact that the divine commandments address in the singular a people who were going to transgress, since the Jewish people also violated precepts given in the singular. For the law is spiritual, and therefore God addressed the people by his divine oracle in one way in his words and in another in his predestination. So he says: You shall not cook a lamb in its mother's milk.

From here on the sequence of the heavenly commands would seem easy, were it not that a great many people raise questions to which we must reply, lest they lead simple minds astray with their malicious interpretation. For many, whose originator is Apelles, as you find in the thirty-eighth book of his work, pose these questions. First: How is it that the tree of life seems to do more for life than the breath of God? Next: If God did not make man perfect, but each person acquires for himself the perfection of virtue by his own effort, does not man seem to acquire more for himself than God bestowed on him? The third objection they raise is this: If man had not tasted death, he certainly could not know what he had not tasted. So if he had not tasted it, he did not know it; and if he did not know it, he could not fear it.

Therefore, they say, God held out death [?] as a threat in vain, since men did not fear it. Let us learn, then, that where God brought forth the tree of life, there he also brought forth the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. For you have it that he brought forth the tree of life "en mesō tou paradeisou," that is, in the middle of paradise. [?] for it is understood that he brought it forth in the middle. So in the middle of paradise there was both life and the cause of death. Understand that man did not make life, but could find it either by working or by guarding God's commandments. Life, however, was, as the apostle said, hidden with Christ in God. Man, then, was either in the shadow of life, by way of figure—for this life of ours now on earth is a shadow—or he was in a kind of pledge of life, since he had the breath of God; he had, therefore, a pledge of immortality. But placed in the shadow of life, he could not see and grasp, by any ordinary touch or sight, the life hidden with Christ in God. Though not yet a sinner, he was nonetheless not of an incorruptible and inviolable nature, seeing that he afterward fell through sin—but he was by no means yet a sinner. Indeed, he was in the shadow of life, whereas sinners are in the shadow of death. For the people of sinners, as Isaiah teaches, sat in the shadow of death, and light arose for them through the grace of God, not through the merit of their own virtue. So there is no difference between the breath of God and the food of the tree of life, nor can anyone say that man can acquire more for himself than was conferred on him by divine generosity. Would that we could hold on to what we received! For our labor serves to recover what was given us. The third question proposed, that one who had not tasted death could not fear death, is easily resolved from ordinary experience of nature. For it is implanted by nature in all living creatures to dread as harmful even things they have not yet experienced as harmful to them. Why else does the sight of a hawk strike terror into a dove from the moment it is hatched? Why are wolves fearsome to sheep, and kites to chicks? If even among irrational creatures there is a natural terror of a hostile kind of animal, so that even irrational beings acquire a sense that death must be fled, how much more should the first man, who was surely most fully endowed with reason, have had a natural sense that death must be avoided!

Again they raise other questions in this way: It is not always wrong to disobey a command. If the command is good, obedience is honorable; but if the command is wicked, it is profitable not to obey. So it is not always wrong to disobey a command; rather, it is wicked to disobey a good command. But the tree that produces knowledge of good and evil is good, since God, too, knows good and evil. Indeed he says: Behold, Adam has become like one of us. If, then, it is good to have the knowledge of good and evil, and the knowledge that God himself has is good, it seems that he who forbids it to men does not forbid it rightly. That is what they propose. But let them understand what it is to know and what force this word has; let them understand it as they should. For the Lord knew those who are his—he knew, that is, those who out of many have been made one, in whom he dwells and among whom he walks. To know, then, would consist not in mere and superficial knowledge, but in doing what ought to be done. Now man ought to have obeyed the command, and by not obeying he transgressed. Therefore he who did not obey went astray, because transgression is sin. And even if they wish to weaken the force of knowing, so as to suppose that what was forbidden was a superficial knowledge of good and evil, in this case too the guilt of transgression lies in not having obeyed the command, since the Lord God judged that even a hasty knowledge of good and evil was to be forbidden.

Another question: He who does not know good and evil is no different from a little child, and in the eyes of a just judge little children bear no guilt. A just maker of the world would never have charged a little child with guilt for not knowing good and evil, since a little child is free of any charge of transgression and guilt. But since we said above that the knowledge of good and evil can be understood in two ways, if we take it as superficial knowledge, then it is certainly false that one who did not know good and evil is no different from a little child. And if it is false that he is no different from a little child, then Adam was not a little child. If he was not a little child, then sin is certainly imputed to him as to one who was not a little child. If sin is imputed, punishment follows sin, since he who could not avoid sin is found deserving of punishment. It may even be that one who does not have knowledge of good and evil is not a little child, since before the child knew good and evil, he did not trust in wickedness. And again you have: Before the child knows how to call father and mother, he will take the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria. So he is perfect who does good, even if he has not acquired knowledge of good and evil, just as many, before they know the law, are a law to themselves. What of the fact that the apostle, before he learned "You shall not covet," did not know that covetousness was evil? Indeed he himself says: I did not know sin except through the law; for I would not have known covetousness had the law not said, "You shall not covet." In this respect even a child can be perfect by the law of nature, before he knows that covetousness is a crime or commits the crime of covetousness. So God willed that man should know, by superficial knowledge, what is evil, lest, as if imperfect, he be unable to avoid it. But by not obeying the command we incur guilt; therefore we acknowledge guilt. If, on the other hand, we mean a high and deep knowledge of good and evil, which deep knowledge indeed makes one perfect, [?] then a little child who could not attain to high and deep knowledge is not on that account rightly condemned as though he were not a little child.

Again they sow questions. He who does not know good and evil, they say, does not even know that it is evil not to keep a command, nor does he know the good itself, which is to obey a command. And so, since he did not know, they say, he who did not obey deserved pardon, not condemnation. This question too finds its answer in what we have already said. For man could have concluded, from what God had already bestowed on him—that he had received the breath of God, that he had been placed in a paradise of delight—that the highest obedience was owed to his maker. And so, even if he did not know the force of good and evil, still, since the author of such great gifts had said that the tree of the knowledge of good and evil must not be tasted, he ought to have kept faith with the one who gave the command; for it was not expertise that was demanded of him, but faith. He certainly understood that God surpasses all things; therefore he ought to have considered who it was that gave the command. Even if he did not understand the force and nature of the commands, he knew nonetheless that reverence was owed to the one who commanded. He had this conviction by nature, even if he did not have the judgment of good and evil. Indeed the woman too says to the serpent: We shall eat of every tree of paradise, but of the fruit of the tree that is in the middle of paradise God said, "You shall not eat of it." She knew, then, that the command must be obeyed, so that she said, "We shall eat of every fruit," as the Lord had ordered, but concerning the tree in the middle of paradise she says that God commanded it not be tasted, lest they die the death. So she who knew that the command must be respected certainly knew that it was evil to transgress, and therefore, having transgressed, she is justly condemned.

Consider another point. If taking from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was so effective that both good and evil came to be known—as Scripture seems to show when it says that when they had both eaten, their eyes were opened and they knew that they were naked, that is, the eyes of the heart were opened and they knew that it was shameful to go about naked—then without doubt, when the woman tasted of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, she sinned and knew that she had sinned. Having known that she had sinned, she ought at least not to have invited her husband to share in the sin. But by enticing her husband and giving him what she herself had tasted, she did not avoid sin but repeated it. For surely, if you look at it rightly, she ought not to have drawn the one she loved into sharing her punishment, but rather to have called him back, even unknowing, from what she herself had recognized to be sin—although this woman, knowing that after her fault she could not remain in paradise, seems to have feared being cast out of paradise alone. In fact, after their fault both hid themselves.

Knowing, then, that she was to be shut out, she did not want to be deprived of the company of the husband she loved. Consider again: knowing evil is not evil, but rather when an act carries out wickedness. For not everyone who knows evil thereby does what is evil, but only he who does what he knows to be evil. Now the incentive to doing what is evil is usually either anger or desire. Nor does one who has knowledge of evil necessarily do what he knows to be wicked, unless he is overcome by either anger or desire. Hence, as we said, the incentive to sin is either anger or desire, or very often fear—although desire arises from fear, as each person wants to avoid what he fears. And so we were right to set down anger and desire as the two incentives of all other vices. Let us consider, then, whether Eve was driven to vice by these goads. But she was neither angry with her husband nor overcome by desire; at least in the second act she errs by giving her husband to eat what she herself had already tasted. At first desire had been the author of her error, so that she herself ate, and it was the cause of the sin that followed. For she could not desire what she had already tasted, and by tasting she had acquired knowledge of evil. The evil she had perceived, therefore, she ought not to have passed on to her husband, nor made her own spouse a transgressor of the divine command. Knowingly and deliberately, then, she sinned; knowingly she drew her husband into her error. Otherwise the word about the tree of the knowledge of good and evil will be found false, if even after she ate of that tree she could not have knowledge of evil. But if the word is true, she certainly could not have had desire as her motive—although many think she should be excused on the ground that, loving her husband, she feared being separated from him, and they put forward this as the motive of her desire: that she wished to be with her husband.

Again another question creeps in: from what source did death befall Adam—from the nature of that tree, or from God? If we ascribe it to the nature of the tree, the fruit of this tree seems to be more powerful than the life-giving breath of God, since the fruit of this tree drew to death the one whom the breath had brought to life. Or if we say that God is the worker of death, they say that we accuse him on two counts: either that he was so harsh that he refused to forgive when he could have forgiven, or, if he could not forgive, that he appears weak. Let us see, then, how this is to be refuted. Unless I am mistaken, the cause of death was disobedience, and therefore man is himself the cause of his own death, and God is not the author of his death. For if a physician prescribes to a sick man what he must avoid, and the man does not think fit to abstain from what is forbidden, the physician is not the cause of his death; rather, he himself is answerable for his own death. So God, like a good physician, forbade Adam to taste what would harm him.

Consider again: to know the good is better than not to know it, and for one who knows the good it is a fine thing to know what is evil, so that he may know how to beware of evil and, being prudent, take the precaution of guarding himself. But on the other hand it is not enough to know only what is evil, lest, once you know evil, you begin to be cheated of the knowledge of the good. It is finer, then, that we know both, so that because we know the good we may flee what is evil, and from the fact that we recognize evil we may prefer the grace of the good. But you ought to know both in such a way that you know them deeply, carry out what you know, and make your actions agree with your knowledge. Otherwise Scripture shows that one who knows neither is more tolerable than one who knows both superficially. For it is a burden to know what you cannot either carry out or avoid; it is a burden to know without the practice and the work of deep understanding. It harms a physician's reputation to know what helps and what harms a sick man unless he uses that knowledge as he should; and so knowledge is not good unless you use it as you should.

Consider this too: not in vain was the tree of the knowledge of good and evil brought forth in the middle of paradise; and if it had been brought forth for just any man, the prohibition would have been superfluous. But it was neither made in vain nor made for anyone other than man, who received the command so that he might use not it alone, but it together with the rest. For if you examine many things, you will find a great many, indeed countless things, that can harm one who does not know how to use them. You will not find even riches profitable if a rich man who has the means for generosity denies food to the poor, shuts out the needy man bereft of help, and extorts what belongs to others because he prevails in power. Beauty itself, and a more pleasing bodily form, often draws people into vice more than ugliness does. Does anyone, then, wish to have ugly rather than handsome children, or desire his children to be poor rather than rich? There are many things of this kind that are to be blamed not on the imprudence of the giver but on the error of the one who misuses them. And therefore it is the user who should be accused rather than the giver.

Here is another question. Did God know that Adam would break his commandments, or did he not? If he did not know, this does not uphold the divine power. But if he knew, and still gave commandments that he knew would be disregarded, then God gave a pointless command, and it is not God's way to command anything pointless. Yet he gave the first-formed [?] Adam a pointless command, since he knew Adam would not keep it. God does nothing pointless, so this scripture is not from God. This is the objection of those who do not accept the Old Testament and who raise such questions. These people, however, must be defeated by their own judgment and belief. Since they do not reject the faith of the New Testament, they must be refuted by an example from it, so that they may believe the Old. When the divine commands and deeds agree with one another, it is clear that both testaments must be believed to come from one author. Let them learn, then, that a commandment given even to one who would break it is neither pointless nor unjust. For the Lord Jesus himself chose Judas, knowing that he would betray him. If they think Judas was chosen through lack of foresight, they belittle the divine power. But they cannot think this, since scripture says that Jesus knew who would betray him. So let these opponents of the Old Testament fall silent.

An answer must also be given to the pagans, in case they raise this objection, for they do not accept an example but demand a reason. Let them too learn why the Son of God gave a commandment to one who would break it and chose one who would betray him. The Lord Jesus had come to save all sinners, so he had to show his will even toward the wicked. Therefore he could not pass over even the one who would betray him. In this way all might see that by choosing even his betrayer he gave a clear sign that he wished to save everyone. Nor was anyone harmed by this: not Adam by receiving a commandment, nor Judas by being chosen. For God did not force the one to transgress or the other to betray, since each could have kept from sin if he had held on to what he had received. Again, he knew that not all the Jews would believe, and yet he says: "I have come only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." So the fault does not lie with the one who commands; the sin lies with the one who transgresses. As far as it rested with God, he showed everyone that he wished to set everyone free. I do not say that he did not know the transgression would happen. On the contrary, I declare that he knew. But that was no reason for him to take on himself the blame that belonged to the betrayer who was perishing, so that the fall of either man might be charged to God. As it is, both stand refuted and convicted. The one received a commandment so that he would not fall. The other was even admitted to the office of apostle, so that the kindness shown him might turn him back from his wish to betray. At the same time, while some are convicted, he would be of benefit to all. For there would be no sin if there had been no prohibition. And without sin there would be no wickedness, and perhaps no virtue either, since virtue could neither exist nor stand out unless there were some seeds of wickedness. For what is sin but breaking the divine law and disobeying the commands of heaven? We do not judge the commands of heaven with the ears of the body. Rather, because the word of God existed, certain notions of good and evil have sprung up in us. By nature we understand that what is evil must be avoided, and by nature we understand that what is good is commanded us. So we seem to hear the voice of the Lord in this, that it forbids some things and commands others. Anyone who does not obey what we have once believed to be commanded by God is judged liable to punishment. But we do not read God's command as though it were written in ink on tablets of stone. We keep it pressed into our hearts by the Spirit of the living God. Our own judgment, then, makes a law for itself. For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature what the law requires, they are a law to themselves even though they do not have the law. They show that the work of the law is written on their hearts. So human judgment is like a law of God to itself.

From this they raise yet another question. We said that the commandment consists in human judgment. In its place they now attack this very judgment, impressed on us by God, as though it were a decree of divine law. "Did the one who created man and impressed these notions of good and evil on him know that man would sin, or did he not?" they ask. If you say he did not know, your view of God is unworthy of his majesty. But suppose you say that God knew man would sin and still impressed on him the common notions of good and evil, so that the mixture of evil kept him from preserving everlasting life. Then you would seem to make God unable to foresee the future in the first case and not good in the second. From this they argue that the human creature was not made by God. We showed above that they say the commandment is not God's. In the same way they say here: "Then the human creature is not from God, since God did not make evil, and man received the notion of evil when he was commanded to keep away from evil things." By this kind of reasoning they try to assert that the good God is one being and the maker of man another. They must be answered at once on their own terms. They will not have man made by God because man is a sinner. They shrink from this view so that the good God will not seem to have made a sinner, since they do not think that anyone who made a sinner is good. Then let them say whether they think the maker of man was made by God. If this maker of man, as they call him, was made by God, how did the good God make a maker of evil? Surely he would not be good. For if he who made a sinner is not good, we must be careful, since it may be even worse to have made the maker of a sinner. The good God ought to have prevented the birth of one who would bring in the substance of sin. But if they say the maker was not begotten, we must ask whether or not the good God could somehow have checked wickedness when it began. If he could not, he is weak; if he could and did not, he is not good. So these views of the heretics do not hold together and do not even agree with one another. Let us therefore ask whether there may have been some reason why God allowed wickedness to enter this world when he could have prevented it, whether that maker was begotten or unbegotten.

Therefore, holding that one and the same God is both good and the Maker, let us establish, if we can, what fits his grace on both counts. Nor let us shy away from the reproach of those who say: "How is God good, when he not only let wickedness enter this world but also allowed it to fall into such great confusion?" This charge would have force if wickedness so infected the strength of the soul and the hidden depths of the inmost mind that it could never be removed, and if the poison of incurable wounds had settled in our mind and soul. Then there would be better ground for this complaint, that although God can do all things, he still let man perish. But our merciful God has kept in store remedies for throwing off error, and he has not taken away the power to wipe out every contagion. So how is it irrational or unjust if he allowed our material nature to be tested by the wavering of human frailty? He did so that grace might later return to man's heart through repentance for his sins, and return with greater interest. Man, aware of his frailty, since he had wavered so easily and strayed from the course of the divine commands, would then fear to lose the heavenly commands, which are like the rudder of a storm-tossed soul. He would credit divine mercy all the more for regaining what he had lost, and would claim some share of the grace for himself because he had turned back.

Now let us consider the reason for this. When God gave man a commandment about that wonderful and blessed life, warning him not to disobey it or he would die the death, why did he think he should give a command about eating and not eating? For some think that such a commandment is entirely unfitting for the creator of heaven and earth and of all things, and entirely unworthy of the inhabitants of paradise, since that life is like the life of the angels. Therefore we cannot suppose that this earthly and perishable food was meant for eating there, since those who neither drink nor eat will be like the angels in heaven. There is no reward in food, since food does not commend us to God. Nor is there great danger in it, since it is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth. So such a command would without doubt seem [?] of so great an author, unless you take this food to be the food the prophet speaks of, which the Lord promises his saints as a great reward: "See, those who serve me shall eat, but you shall go hungry." This is the food in which eternal life consists, and whoever is deprived of it will die the death, since the Lord himself is the living, heavenly bread that gives life to this world. That is why he himself also says: "Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have eternal life." So there was a certain bread that he had told the inhabitants of paradise to eat. What bread was it? Hear what scripture calls it: "Man ate the bread of angels." For it is good bread, if you do the will of God. Do you want to know how good this bread is? The Son himself eats it, for he says of it: "My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven."

Next let us see why the Lord God said to Adam, "You shall die by death." What is the difference between saying "you shall die" and adding "you shall die by death"? For we must show that nothing in God's commandment is superfluous. This is what I think. Death and life are opposites. In plain speech we say that one lives from life and dies from death. But you may wish to double each term. Because life produces life, we say "life lives," as you find in the law. And because death produces death, we say "he shall die by death." This doubling is not superfluous. For there is a life that leads to death and a death that leads to life, since whoever lives is dying while he lives, and is living while he dies. So we arrive at four distinctions: to live by life, to die by death, to die by life, and to live by death. Since this is so, we must set aside the bias of usage and habit. Ordinary usage uses "to live" for both the one who lives by life and the one who lives by death. In the same way it uses "to die" both for the one who dies by death and for the one who dies by life. Thus out of the four it expresses only two. It says that the living person lives, without distinguishing better from worse, and that the dying person dies, with no apparent distinction between a bad death and a good one. What it expresses is life without distinction, such as the life of irrational creatures or even of small children, and likewise death without distinction.

So let us set common usage aside and consider what it is to live by life, to die by death, to live by death and to die by life. I think that, according to the Scriptures, to live by life means that wonderful and blessed life. It seems to show this ordinary use of living and gift of breath joined, as it were, with the grace of the blessed life, and mingled with it by a kind of participation. For to live by life is to live by virtue, to carry out the actions of the blessed life in the life of this body. On the other hand, what is dying by death? It means that besides the death of the body there is the ugliness of one who dies in such a way that his flesh loses the common gift of living and his soul cannot enjoy eternal life. There is also the one who dies by life: he lives in the body but dies by his own conduct. Such are those who, as the prophet says, go down alive into hell, and the woman of whom the apostle says that she is dead even while she lives. The fourth remains: there are those who live even by death, like the holy martyrs, who die precisely so that they may live. Their flesh dies, but the grace of the dead lives on. Far be it from us, then, to live as sharers in death. Rather, let us die as sharers in life. For the saint does not even want to share in this life, as he says: "to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better." And another says: "Woe is me, that my sojourn has been prolonged." He grieves, of course, that while he hopes for the fellowship of eternal life, he is held back by the frailty of this life. So I can also put it the other way round: although to live by life is good, to live for life is ambiguous. In one sense someone may be said to live for life, meaning that in the life of this body he serves as a soldier for eternal life. In another sense someone may be said to live for life, meaning that he desires this bodily life, whether he is an ordinary person or a saint. For example, someone may think he should live upright so that his good deeds will earn him a long life. Many of the weaker sort, who take delight in this life, are like this.

We have learned what it is to live for life. Let us now learn what it is to die to death or to live for death. For there can be those who die to death and those who live for life. Whoever does not live in a way that leads to the death of his soul dies to death. Because he is not liable to death, the bond of wretched death has lost its hold on him, and he is not bound by the chains of eternal death. He has died to death; that is, he has died to sin and died to punishment. The opposite of this is to live for punishment, that is, when one who lives for punishment lives for death. And one who dies for punishment dies for death. There is also one who, while still in this life, dies for life, like the man who said: "I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me." For he died to sin and lives to God. That is, death has died in him, but Life lives in him, and that Life is the Lord Jesus. So the life of those who live to God is good, and the life of those who live to sin is bad. There is also an intermediate life, like that of the other living creatures, as you find written: "Let the earth bring forth living souls according to their kind." There is also a life of the dead, as with the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob, for he is not the God of the dead but of the living. There are also some who share in both death and life, of whom the apostle speaks when he says: "If you have died with him, you will also live with him." For he says, "If we have been planted together with him in the likeness of his death, we shall also share in his resurrection. We know that our old self was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed and we might no longer be slaves to sin. For whoever has died has been justified from sin." Just as we have described many forms of life, so we shall find many forms of death. Death is called evil, as in the saying: "The soul that sins shall itself die." Death is also used in the ordinary sense, as when you read, for example, that [Adam] lived so many years and died and was gathered to his fathers. Death is also spoken of in connection with the sacrament of baptism, as you have it: "For we were buried with him through baptism into death." And elsewhere: "But if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him." You see that this is called death, yet it is our life.

Here is another question, arising from the Lord's saying that it is not good for man to be alone. First of all, notice that earlier, where God formed man from the clay of the earth, he did not add "God saw that it was good," as he did with each of his other works. If scripture had said there that it was good that man had been made, this passage would turn out to contradict it, since here it says that it was not good after having said above that it was good. But note that this holds for the place where he made Adam alone. Where scripture covers the making of man and woman together, it does not say so specifically even there. Still, it goes on to say, "God saw all that he had made, and behold, it was very good." This clearly declares that it is good that both man and woman were made.

But this question has raised yet another one. Why was it not said that it was good that Adam was made when he was made alone, while once the woman too was made from him, all things were included together as good? Scripture there praised the whole of creation, and the creation of the universe was approved, since the nature shared by all creation was praised in man. Still, it does not seem idle to ask why, where Adam alone was made, not only was no word of approval added to a work that pleased God, but it was even said that it is not good for man to be alone. We know that Adam did not go astray before the woman was made. But after the woman was made, she was the first to break the divine command, and she drew her husband into error as well and became his temptation. If, then, the woman caused the man's guilt, how can she seem to have been added for good? Yet if you consider that God cares for the whole of creation, you will find that what held the cause of the whole was bound to please the Lord more than what held the cause of sin was bound to be condemned. And so, because the human race could not be propagated from the man alone, the Lord declared that it is not good for man to be alone. For God preferred that there be many whom he could save and whose sins he could forgive, rather than only one, Adam, who would be free from guilt. Indeed, since he is the author of both works, he came into this world to save sinners. Finally, he did not even let Cain, guilty of murdering his brother, perish before he had fathered sons. So the woman had to be added to the man so that the human race could continue from generation to generation. Indeed, the very words of God declare this when he says that it is not good for man to be alone. For although the woman was going to sin first, she was also going to give birth to her own redemption, so she ought not to be shut out from God's work. Adam was not deceived, while the woman was deceived and fell into transgression. Yet, as scripture says, she will be saved through bearing children, and among those she bore was Christ.

Nor is it without purpose that the woman was made not from the same earth from which Adam was formed, but from Adam's own rib. This was so that we might know that man and woman share one bodily nature and that the human race has one source. That is why, in the beginning, man and woman were not made as two separate beings, nor were two men made, nor two women. First the man was made, and then the woman from him. For God wished to establish a single nature for human beings, and by beginning this creation from a single origin he removed the possibility of many different natures. "Let us make him a helper like himself," he says. We understand this as a helper in the begetting of the human race, and truly a good helper. If you take "helper" to mean the better partner, then in begetting the woman is found to do the greater work. She is like the earth, which first receives the seeds and holds them, makes them grow little by little with its warmth, and brings them forth as a crop. In this, then, the woman is a good helper, even though a helper is also called the inferior partner. We find this in human practice too, since people of higher rank often take on someone of lower standing [?] as their helper.

Now consider why God went on to form from the earth all the beasts of the field and all the birds of the sky and brought them to Adam, to see what he would call them. Why was this done, when God brought only the beasts of the field and the birds of the sky to Adam? For there were also cattle according to their kind. Indeed, you find below that Adam gave names to all the cattle and to all the beasts of the field, but for Adam no helper like him was found. What is the answer, then, except that the untamed beasts and the birds of the sky are brought to man by divine power, while man himself also had the power to gather the tame cattle? So the one was the work of God, the other of human effort. At the same time, understand why all of them were brought to Adam. It was so that he might see that in all of them nature consists of both sexes, male and female. He would then learn from experience and example that the companionship of a woman had been given him as something he needed.

"And God," it says, "cast a deep sleep upon Adam, and he slept." What is this sleep? For a little while, when we turn our minds to marriage, our eyes are fixed on the kingdom of God, yet we seem to bend and turn them toward a kind of sleep of this world. For a little while we fall asleep to divine things as we rest in worldly and secular affairs. Then, after he cast a deep sleep upon Adam, it says, and he slept, "the Lord God built the rib that he had taken from Adam into a woman." Scripture rightly said "built" when it spoke of the making of the woman, because a household seems to reach its full completion in man and woman. A man without a wife is regarded as being without a home. For just as the man is thought better suited to public duties, so the woman is thought better suited to the tasks of the household. Note that he took a rib from the body, not a portion from the soul, that is:

not soul from soul, but “bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called woman.” So we have learned the cause of human generation. But many who look into it more carefully are troubled by this question. Placing human beings in paradise was either God's great gift to them at the very beginning, or else, later, seems to be the reward for great merits, since every righteous person is caught up into paradise. How, then, can beasts and cattle of the field and birds of the air also be said to have been in paradise? For this reason many have held that paradise is the human soul, in which certain seeds of the virtues have sprouted, and that the man was placed there both to work and to guard paradise; that is, the man is the human mind. Its power seems to cultivate the soul, and not only to cultivate it, but also, once it has cultivated it, to guard it. The beasts of the field and the birds of the air that are brought to Adam are our irrational impulses, since the beasts or cattle are the various passions of the body, some more turbulent, some more sluggish. And what else do we take the birds of the air to be but empty thoughts, which flutter around our soul like birds and often carry it off this way and that with their shifting motion? That is why no helper like our mind was found except sense, that is, αἴσθησις. This alone could our [?] find similar to itself.

But perhaps you will object that God also placed these things in such a paradise, that is, the passions of the body and a certain emptiness of wavering or idle thoughts, and so was himself the author of our error. Consider what he says: “Have dominion over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air and all creeping things that creep upon the earth.” You see that he gave you dominion, so that you might judge all things and distinguish the kinds of each by the sober determination of your judgment. God called all things to you so that you might know that your mind is above all things. Why did you choose to take to yourself and join to yourself things you had found to be in no way like you? He certainly gave you sense, by which you might know all things and judge what you knew; and you were rightly cast out of that fruitful field of paradise, because you could not keep the commandment. For God knew that you were frail; he knew that you could not judge. That is why he said, as to the frailer ones: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.” Since, then, he knew you were too weak to judge, he wanted you to be obedient to his command, and for this reason he laid down a precept. If you had not transgressed it, you could not have fallen into the danger of an uncertain judgment. So, because you wanted to judge, he added: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil.” You wanted to claim judgment for yourself; you must not refuse the penalty of perverse judgment.

Yet he placed you opposite paradise, so that you could not wipe out its memory. Indeed, the righteous are caught up into paradise, as Paul was caught up into paradise and heard unspeakable words. You too may be caught up by the vigor of your mind from the first heaven to the second, and from the second heaven to the third. That is, every human being is first bodily, second natural, third spiritual. If you are caught up to the third heaven in this way, so as to see the brightness of spiritual grace (for the natural man does not know the things of the Spirit, and so the ascent to the third heaven is necessary for you, that you may be caught up into paradise), you will now be caught up without danger, so that you can judge all things, since the spiritual man judges all things but is himself judged by no one. And perhaps, being still frail, you will hear unspeakable words which it is not lawful for a man to utter; then keep what you have received and guard what you have heard. The apostle Paul guarded them, so that he would not fall or cause others to go astray. Or perhaps Paul said, “which it is not lawful for a man to utter,” because he was still in the body; that is, he saw the passions of this body, he saw the law of his flesh warring against the law of his mind. I prefer to understand it this way, so that we may not seem to be brandishing the terror of some danger still to come; let there be security at least for this life, so that we need fear no snares of future transgression from then on. So whoever has been in paradise by the ascent of virtue will hear those hidden and secret mysteries of God; he will hear the Lord saying to him, as to that thief who turned from crime to confession and from robbery to faith: “Today you will be with me in paradise.”

“Now the serpent was wiser than all the beasts that were on the earth, which the Lord God had made. And the serpent said to the woman: Why has God said that you are not to eat of every tree that is in paradise?” When he calls the serpent wiser, you understand whom he means, namely our adversary, who nonetheless has the wisdom of this world. But pleasure and delight can also fittingly be called wise, because there is also what is called the wisdom of the flesh, as you have it that “the wisdom of this flesh is hostile to God”; and those who crave pleasures are cunning in seeking out kinds of delight. If, then, you understand it as delight, it is something opposed to the divine command and hostile to our senses, which is why Saint Paul says: “I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin.” But if you refer it to the devil, he is the true enemy of the human race. And what is the cause of enmity but envy? As Solomon says, “Through the envy of the devil death entered the world.” The cause of envy was the happiness of man placed in paradise. Because the devil himself could not keep the grace he had received, he envied man, since man, though formed from mud, had been chosen to dwell in paradise. For the devil considered that he, who had been of a higher nature, had fallen into these worldly and earthly things, while man, a lower creature, was hoping for eternal things. This, then, is why he envied, saying: “Shall this inferior being obtain what I could not keep? Shall he move from earth to heaven, when I have fallen from heaven to earth? I have many ways by which I can deceive man. He was made from mud, the earth is his mother, he is wrapped in corruptible things. Even if his soul is of a higher nature, it too, placed in the prison of the body, can be liable to fall, since I could not avoid falling. So the first way is to deceive him while he desires things greater than his condition allows; for this is a kind of striving of enterprise. Next, it belongs to the flesh to desire what it does not have. Finally, in what way do I seem wiser than all, unless I outwit man and contend with craft and fraud?” So he contrived not to attack Adam first, but to try to outwit Adam through the woman. He did not attack the one who had received the heavenly command in person, but attacked her who had learned from her husband, not received from God, what she was to observe. For you do not read that God spoke to the woman, but that he spoke to Adam, and so the woman must be thought to have learned it through Adam.

Once you recognize the kind of temptation in this passage, you will find many other kinds of temptation in other passages as well. Some come through the prince of this world, who has spewed certain poisons of wisdom into this world, so that people think false things are true and human affections are captured by a kind of outward show. For he does not always come in as an open enemy; there are certain powers that feign love and put on a show of favor, so that little by little they may pour the poison of their wickedness into our thoughts. From them arise those sins that spring either from delight or from a certain pliancy of mind. There are also other powers that wrestle with us, as it were. That is why the apostle says: “For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers and the rulers of this world, of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.” By this kind of contest they want to break us and, as it were, crush the body of our soul. So Paul, like a good athlete, had learned not only to avoid the blows of the opposing powers, but also to strike his opponents. That is why he says: “I strike with my fists, not as one beating the air.” And so, as a good athlete, he was found worthy to reach the crown. The devil's temptations, then, are manifold. That is why the serpent is regarded as double-tongued and deadly, because the devil's servant says one thing with his tongue and plots another in his heart. There are also other servants who hurl the arrows of their words, as it were, poisoned with the venom of both heart and voice; to them the Lord says: “Brood of vipers, how can you speak good things when you are evil?”

“And the serpent said to the woman: Why has God said, You are not to eat of every tree that is in paradise? And the woman said to the serpent: We shall eat of every tree of paradise; but of the fruit of the tree that is in the middle of paradise God said, You shall not eat of it, nor shall you touch it, lest you die.” When you hear that the serpent is wiser than all the beasts, look here for his cunning. He pretends to be repeating the words of God and weaves in tricks of his own. For God had said: “You shall eat of every tree that is in paradise for food, but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat; on the day you eat of it you shall surely die.” God had said, “You shall eat of every tree that is in paradise, but of one tree you shall not eat,” yet the serpent, as though questioning the woman, slipped in a lie, saying, “You are not to eat of every tree,” when God had commanded that only the one tree of the knowledge of good and evil was not to be tasted. It is no wonder that he deceived in this way, since it is the habit of those who try to outwit someone to deceive. So the serpent's question is not idle. But so that you may know that there could be no fault in the command, the woman answered and said: “We shall eat of every tree of paradise; but of the fruit of the tree that is in the middle of paradise God said, You shall not eat of it, nor shall you touch it, lest you surely die.” There is no fault in the command itself, but in the reporting of the command. For, as far as the present reading teaches, we learn that we must add nothing to a command, not even for the sake of caution. If you either add or take away anything, it seems a kind of transgression of the command. The pure and simple form of a command must be preserved, and the sequence of testimony must be reported faithfully. Often, when a witness adds something of his own to the account of events, he discolors the whole credibility of his testimony by a lie in one part. Nothing, then, should be added, not even what seems good. What offense does the woman's addition, “nor shall you touch anything of it,” seem to have at first sight? For God had not said “you shall touch,” but “you shall not eat.” And yet it is the beginning of the fall. For what she added was either superfluous, or by adding something of her own she took God's command to be incomplete. So the sequence of the present reading teaches us that we must neither take anything away from the divine commands nor add to them. For if John [?] concerning his own writings: “If anyone adds to these things, God will add to him the plagues that are written in this book; and if anyone takes away from the words of this prophecy, God will take away his share from the book of life,” how much more must nothing be taken away from the divine commands! Here, then, the first transgression of the command began. Many think this fault was not the woman's but Adam's: that Adam, wanting to make her more cautious, told the woman that God had commanded, “nor shall you touch anything of it.” For we have it that Adam, not Eve, received the command from God, since the woman had not yet been formed. The reading does not record the actual words in which Adam told the woman the form and wording of the command, but we understand that the wording of the command passed to the woman through the man. I shall consider what others think; but to me it seems that the fault began with the woman, that she started the lie. For even if it seems uncertain which of the two it was, the sex reveals which one could have erred first. Add that she is bound by a presumption against her, since she was afterward found to have erred first. For the woman was the author of error to the man, not the man to the woman. That is why Paul says: “Adam was not deceived, but the woman was seduced into transgression.”

Now let us see whether, apart from the addition attached to the command, what was added seems to have done harm. For if “nor shall you touch it” really is good and served for caution, why did God not forbid this, and indeed seem to have permitted it by not forbidding it? So both questions must be asked: why he neither permitted it nor forbade it. For there are those who say: why did he not order what he made to be seen also to be touched? But when you hear that the nature of the knowledge of good and evil was in that tree, it can be supposed that he did not want you to touch evil. For it is enough for us to see Satan falling like lightning from heaven, according to the Lord's word, and giving food not to the children of light but to the children of night and darkness, since it is written: “He gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia.” This, then, has been said about why he did not command it to be touched; now hear what I understand about why he did not forbid it.
