There are many things that harm us if we choose to take them in before we know what they are. This often happens with food and drink: if you know beforehand that something is bitter, you will put on patience, and if you understand that bitter things do good, you will put on endurance, so that sudden bitterness does not upset you and make you begin to reject what would do you good. So it is useful to know beforehand, so that, from knowing that a thing will do you good, you do not loathe even bitter things.

But these things can do less harm; notice what can do more harm unless one takes precautions. Here is a pagan: he is moving toward the faith. He is a catechumen and wants to receive a fuller measure of doctrine and faith. Let him beware lest, in wanting to learn, he learn badly, and learn from Photinus, learn from Arius, learn from Sabellius, handing himself over to teachers of this sort, whose authority may draw him on. Led on by a certain presumption of his teachers, pressed upon his tender mind, he may not know how to judge. So let him first look with the eyes of the mind at what he is following; let him see where life is; let him then touch the life-giving substance of the divine readings, so that he may not be tripped up by a perverse interpreter. Sabellius reads to him: “I am in the Father and the Father in me,” and says there is one person. Photinus reads: “the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus,” and elsewhere: “Why do you seek to kill me, a man?” Arius too reads that he said: “for the Father is greater than I.” What is read is indeed plain, but he ought first to consider carefully in himself why it was said, so that he may grasp the reason for the words. He is led by the authority of his teachers, and it would have been better for him not to have sought at all than to have found such a teacher. Likewise, if some pagan takes up the Scriptures, he reads: “an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth”; he also reads: “if your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off.” He does not understand the meaning, he does not perceive the hidden things of the divine word, and he falls worse than if he had not read at all. And so John taught how they ought to search into the word of God: not superficially, not carelessly, but diligently and with care. “That which was from the beginning,” he says, “which we have heard and which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon and our hands have examined, concerning the word of life: we have seen and we testify and we proclaim to you.” You see that he first examined the word of God with hands, as it were, and afterward proclaimed it. And so perhaps the word would have done Adam and Eve no harm, if they had first touched it, handling it carefully with the hands, so to speak, of the mind. For the weak, by handling and inquiring more carefully, can search out the nature of each thing they do not understand. Certainly, being weak, they ought first to have examined how they should touch that tree in which they knew the knowledge of evil lay. For even the knowledge of evil can often benefit us. And so we read of the devil's frauds, whether in this reading or in prophecy, so that we may learn how to guard against his arts; for his temptations must be known, not that we may follow them, but that, taught and instructed, we may guard against them.

There are some who are in doubt at this point whether God said that every tree was to be tasted in such a way that the tree of the knowledge of good and evil might be tasted along with every tree, or whether he said that every tree was to be tasted and only the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was not to be tasted. They think it not unreasonable to suppose that, although the food of this tree was harmful, it could not be harmful if it were eaten with the others. For they say that the antidote theriac is usually made from the body of a serpent: the venom and body of the serpent, taken alone, certainly harm, but mixed with other things they make for health and well-being. So too the knowledge of good and evil is by no means considered useless if one has wisdom, if one is always intent on life, if one attains the other kinds of virtue. For this reason many had thought it could also be understood that God forbade the tree of the knowledge of good and evil to be tasted alone, apart from the others, but did not forbid it together with the others. And they think this was said because God said to Adam: “Who told you that you were naked, unless you have eaten of the tree of which I commanded you that of this alone you should not eat?” This would seem to leave some room for interpretation, had not the woman, earlier, when the serpent said, “Why has God said that you are not to eat of every tree that is in paradise?”, answered: “Of the tree that is in the middle of paradise God said, You shall not eat of it.” In this, although the testimony of the woman, who was about to transgress, seems rather weak, still I will not strip Adam of all virtues, as though he had attained no virtue in paradise, had tasted nothing of the other trees, and had fallen into guilt before gaining any fruits. I will not strip Adam, then, lest I strip the whole human race, which is innocent before it receives the sense of the knowledge of good and evil. For it was not said idly: “Unless you turn and become like this child, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.” For a child, when cursed, does not curse back; when struck, does not strike back; he knows nothing of the temptations of ambition and plunder.

So I think it truer that he commanded that the tree was not to be eaten even with the other fruits. For although knowledge is good for the perfect, it is useless for the imperfect. I would dare to call every human being imperfect, since Paul himself speaks as one imperfect: “Not that I have already received it or am already perfect, but I press on to lay hold of it.” And so the Lord says to the imperfect: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.” Knowledge, then, is useless to the imperfect. Thus: “I did not know sin, except that the law said, You shall not covet”; and below: “For apart from the law sin is dead.” What good was it to me to know what I could not avoid? What good was it to me to know what the law of my flesh would fight against? Paul is under attack and sees the law of his flesh warring against the law of his mind and making him captive to the law of sin; he does not presume on his own conscience, but trusts that through the grace of Christ he will be set free from the body of death. And do you suppose that anyone who has knowledge cannot sin? Paul says: “For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want, that I do.” And do you think knowledge benefits a person, when it increases the odium of the offense? Granted, however, that the perfect cannot sin: in Adam God foresaw all human beings, and therefore it was not fitting for the human race as a whole to have the knowledge of good and evil, which, because of the vices of the flesh, it could not exercise as it ought.

Let us learn, then, that the devil's temptations are full of lies; for scarcely one of the things he promised seems true; the rest he made up falsely. For this is what you have: “And the serpent said to the woman: You shall not surely die.” There is one falsehood; for man, who followed the serpent's promises, did surely die. Then he added: “For God knew that on whatever day you eat of it, your eyes will be opened.” This alone is true, for below you have that they both ate and their eyes were opened; but this was a truth that would do harm. Indeed, it is not useful for everyone to have their eyes opened, for it is written: “They will see and not see.” But at once a lie was glued on, for he added: “and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.” Here we may observe that the serpent is the author of idolatry, since it was a piece of the serpent's cunning that seems to have led people into the error of many gods. And in this too he deceived, saying that man would be like gods; for not only did human beings cease to be like gods, but even those who were like gods, to whom it was said, “I said: You are gods,” lost their grace.

“And the woman saw that the tree was good to eat, and that it was pleasing to the eyes to see and beautiful to behold.” She was a weak author of judgment, judging about what she had not tasted. And so, it seems, nothing should readily be taken up for any action unless we have examined it more carefully and tested it with our inner feeling. “Taking of its fruit,” it says, “she ate, and gave also to her husband with her, and they both ate.” It is fitting that the moment when Adam is deceived is passed over, since he fell not by his own fault but through the fault of his wife.

"And their eyes were opened," it says, "and they knew that they were naked." They had been naked before, it is true, but not without the coverings of the virtues. They were naked because their ways were simple and because their nature knew no cloak of deceit. Now, however, the human mind is veiled in many wrappings of pretense. So once they saw that they had been stripped of the sincerity and simplicity of an intact and uncorrupted nature, they began to look for worldly and handmade things with which to cover the nakedness of their minds. They sewed delights to delights and the shadowy pleasures of this world to one another, like leaves to leaves, so as to shade their private parts. For how could Adam have had the eyes of his body closed, when he saw all living creatures so clearly that he even gave them names? How, then, did they know? By an inner and higher knowledge they knew that what they lacked was not a tunic but the coverings of the virtues.

"And they sewed fig leaves," it says, "and made themselves aprons." How we ought to understand the fig in this passage is taught by the sequence of the divine readings. Scripture records that those who rest under the vine and the fig tree are holy, and Solomon said, "Who plants a fig tree and does not eat its fruit?" The Lord, too, came to the fig tree and was displeased because he found no fruit on it, only leaves. Adam, then, teaches me what leaves are: after he sinned, he made himself an apron of fig leaves, when he ought rather to have tasted its fruit. The just man chooses the fruit; the sinner chooses the leaves. What is the fruit? "The fruit of the Spirit," it says, "is charity, joy, peace, patience, kindness, modesty, continence, love." He who had no joy did not have the fruit. He who had broken God's command did not have faith. He who had tasted of the tree forbidden to him did not have continence.

So whoever breaks God's command is stripped and laid bare and becomes shameful to himself. He wants to cover himself with fig leaves of some kind, perhaps with empty or shadowy words. The sinner sews these together with contrived lies, building word on word, and weaves them into a veil to cover the conscience of his mind and his deed, so as to hide his shameful parts. For anyone who wishes to veil his fault throws leaves over himself: he names the devil as the author of his offense, or pleads the allurements of the flesh, or points to someone else as the one who talked him into error. He often brings out examples from the divine Scriptures to claim that the just also fell into sin. If he has been caught in debauchery, he may say, "Abraham too lay with a slave girl, and David fell in love with another man's wife and took her for himself." He sews onto himself examples from the prophetic Scriptures, but he does not think their fruit worth looking for.

Do not the Jews also seem to you to be sewing leaves when they interpret the words of the spiritual law in a bodily sense? Their interpretation loses all the fruit of its greenness, condemned by the curse of eternal barrenness. Good interpretation, then, is the spiritual fig tree. It bears fruit, and the just and holy rest beneath it. Whoever plants it in the souls of individuals will eat its fruit, as Paul says: "I planted, Apollos watered." Bad interpretation, however, can neither bear fruit nor keep its greenness.

What is more serious is that Adam girded himself with this interpretation in the very place where he ought rather to have girded himself with the fruit of chastity. For the seeds of generation are said to lie in the loins, where we are girded. So Adam was wrongly girded there with useless leaves, since he marked out not the fruit that future generations would bear but certain sins, and these remained until the coming of the Lord and Savior. But when the Lord came, he found the fig tree uncultivated. When he was asked not to order it cut down, he allowed it to be cultivated. And so we are now girded not with leaves but with the divine word, for the Lord himself says, "Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning." That is also why he forbids us to carry money in our belts: our belt should hold not the things of this world but the things that are eternal.

"And they heard," it says, "the voice of the Lord walking about toward evening." What is this walking of God, who is always everywhere? I think God walks, as it were, through the sequence of the divine Scriptures, in which his presence dwells in a certain way. We hear that he sees all things, and that "the eyes of the Lord are on the just"; we read that Jesus knew their thoughts; we read, "Why do you think evil in your hearts?" When we go over these things, we recognize God as if he were walking about. The sinner, then, had fled. He did not go somewhere he could escape God's sight; rather, he wanted to hide within his own conscience and did not want his works to come into the light. For the just see face to face, because the mind of the just man is not only present to God but even reasons with God, as it is written: "Judge for the orphan and vindicate the widow, and come, let us reason together, says the Lord." So when the sinner reads these Scriptures, he hears the voice of God as of one walking toward evening. What does "toward evening" mean, except that he recognizes his guilt late? The shame for past error comes late, when it ought to have forestalled the error. For while guilt burns hot in the body and the soul is stirred up by the body's passions, the mind of one who has gone astray does not think of God. That is, it does not hear God walking in the divine Scriptures and walking in the minds of each of us. For God says, "I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God." So when fear of the divine power has come back into the soul's awareness, then we blush and long to hide ourselves. Then, caught up in thoughts of our sins, we are found in the midst of the tree of paradise where we sinned, wanting to hide and supposing that God does not search out hidden things. But he who searches souls and thoughts, and pierces even to the dividing of the soul, says:

"Adam, where are you?" How does God speak? With a bodily voice? Certainly not. He pours out his oracles by a power far superior to any bodily voice. The prophets heard this voice of his, and the faithful hear it, but the ungodly do not understand it. So in the Gospel you find that the evangelist heard the Father saying, "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again," but the Jews did not hear. Instead they said, "It thundered." Earlier God was perceived to be walking about when he was not walking, and in the same way here God was heard speaking when he was not speaking.

But let us consider what he says: "Adam, where are you?" For those who hear the word of God, these words still hold a remedy that can heal them. The Jews, who closed their ears so as not to hear, do not deserve to hear even today. Next, those who hid themselves have a remedy. For whoever hides is ashamed, and whoever is ashamed turns back, as it is written: "Let them all be put to shame and turned back very quickly." Next, the very fact that he calls shows that he means to heal, for the Lord calls those on whom he has mercy. In saying "Where are you?" he who knows what is hidden is not asking about a place. God did not have his eyes closed, unable to see the one who was hiding. Indeed, he said, "Adam has become like one of us," precisely because Adam's eyes had been opened. He opened his eyes, to be sure, so that he saw his own guilt, which he had not managed to avoid. Somehow we recognize our offenses better after we have sinned. Then we understand that something is a sin which we did not think was a sin before we committed it, or at least did not think deserved condemnation as a sin; for if we had condemned it, we would not have done it. But God sees everyone's faults and knows everyone's offenses. His eyes are on the souls of all and on all their secrets. Why, then, "Adam, where are you?" That is, not "In what place are you?" but "In what condition are you?" It is not a question but a rebuke. "From what good things," he says, "from what blessedness, from what grace have you fallen, and into what misery? You have abandoned eternal life and been entombed in death, buried along with error. Where is that confidence of yours that came from a good conscience? This fear confesses your guilt; this hiding place confesses your transgression. Where are you, then? I am not asking in what place you are, but in what state. Where have your sins brought you, that you flee from your God, whom you once sought?" Someone may wonder why Adam is rebuked first, when the woman tasted first. The answer is that the weaker sex began the transgression and the stronger sex began the shame and the excuse, so that the woman was the cause of error and the man the cause of shame.

"And the woman said, 'The serpent deceived me, and I ate.'" A fault that is followed by confession of the offense can be pardoned. So the woman was not given up as hopeless: she did not keep silent before God but confessed her sin, and a healing sentence followed. It is good to be condemned for our sin and scourged for our wrongdoing, so that we may be scourged with men. Cain, for instance, wanted to deny his crime, and so he was judged unworthy to be punished for his sin and was sent away without any sentence of punishment. Perhaps this was not so much because of the greater crime of fratricide, which he committed against his brother, as because of his sacrilege, for he thought he could lie to God, saying, "I do not know; am I my brother's keeper?" So his accusation was reserved for the devil, the accuser, so that he who refused to be scourged with men would be scourged with the devil's angels. Of such people it is said, "There is no turning aside from their death, and they will not be scourged with men." The woman's case is different. Although she had fallen into the guilt of transgression, she still had the food of virtue from the trees of paradise. So she declared her sin, and it was counted to her for pardon. For "the just man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech"; no one can be justified from sin unless he has first confessed it. That is why the Lord says, "Tell your iniquities, so that you may be justified."

Because Eve herself confessed her offense, a milder and beneficial sentence followed. It condemned her error but did not deny her pardon: she was to turn to her husband and serve him. This was first so that she would not easily take pleasure in going astray, and second so that, placed under the stronger vessel, she would not lead her husband astray but would rather be guided by his counsel. In this I clearly recognize the mystery of Christ and the Church. For it points to the Church's future turning to Christ, and to a religious servitude subject to the word of God that is far better than the freedom of this world. So it is written: "You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone." This servitude, then, is a gift of God. Indeed, the obedience of this servitude is counted among the blessings, for Isaac gave it to his son Esau in place of a blessing, that he should serve his brother. Esau had in fact asked for a blessing. Though he knew that one blessing had been snatched from him, he still asked for another, saying, "Have you only one blessing, father?" Earlier he had sold his birthright out of gluttony and lost the grace of the blessing through his passion for hunting in the wild. Now he believed that this servitude would make him better, if he revered the type of Christ in his brother. For the Christian people are strong in this servitude, as the Lord said to his disciples: "Whoever wishes to be first among you must be the servant of all." Indeed, this servitude is the work of charity, which is greater than hope and faith. So it is written: "Through charity serve one another." This, then, is the mystery the Apostle speaks of concerning Christ and the Church. She was truly in transgression before, but she will be saved through bearing children in faith and charity and holiness with chastity. The human race, which had transgressed in the fathers, is saved through the children, so that what had gone wrong among the Jews might be set right in the Christian descendants.

"The serpent persuaded me," she says. God considered this pardonable, because he knew that the serpent has many ways of deceiving. He transforms himself into an angel of light, and his ministers appear like ministers of justice. He gives each thing a false name, calling rashness courage and giving avarice the name of industry. For the serpent deceived the woman, and the woman led the man away from the truth into transgression. The serpent stands for bodily pleasure. The woman is a symbol of our senses, the man of the mind. Pleasure moves the senses, and the senses pass on to the mind the passion they have received. Pleasure, therefore, is the first origin of sin. So do not be surprised that God's judgment condemns the serpent first, the woman second, and the man third. The order of condemnation follows the order of the error, for pleasure usually takes the senses captive, and the senses the mind. To see that the serpent is a type of pleasure, consider its condemnation.

"On your breast," it says, "and on your belly you shall go." Who are those who go on their belly but those who live for the belly and the gullet, "whose god is their belly and whose glory is in their shame," who set their minds on earthly things and, weighed down with food, are bent toward the earth? So he speaks fittingly to pleasure, which, intent on food, seems to eat earth: "On your breast and on your belly you shall go, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life." Every excuse must be taken away from the devil, so that he cannot plead anything in defense of his malice. He might say that his wickedness came to him from his condemnation, and that he works so stubbornly to harm men because he was condemned for the very purpose of doing harm. That would seem close to plausible if we took this sentence as a condemnation. But God did not condemn the serpent so that it would do harm; he showed what would happen. Indeed, we have shown above that this temptation is actually of benefit to men. Still, if we recognize that it is written, with God speaking, "Those who honor me I will honor, and he who despises me will be deprived of honor," we can draw a conclusion from these words. God works what is good, not what is evil. So let the divine words teach you that he works glory and leaves punishment aside. "Those who honor me," he says, "I will honor," declaring that the honor of the good is his own work. "And those who despise me," he says. He did not say "I will deprive of honor" but "will be deprived of honor." He did not count their disgrace as his own work but showed what would happen. So here he did not say, "I make you go on your breast and belly and eat earth all the days of your life," but "you shall go" and "you shall eat." In this way he appears to have foretold what would happen to the serpent rather than prescribed what it should do. "Earth," he says, "will be your food, not the soul"; for even this benefits sinners. That is why the Apostle handed over such a man "for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ." He says that the serpent crawls on its breast and belly not so much because of the shape of its body as because it fell from that heavenly blessing through earthly thoughts. For the breast is often taken as a kind of inner chamber of wisdom. That is why the apostle rests his head on Christ's breast and does not cast it down to the earth. The wisdom of the devil is compared to the most savage beasts, whose breast lies between their feet. Men too who set their minds on earthly things, and are not raised toward heaven by any inner affection, seem to crawl over the earth on their belly. If so, we certainly ought not to fill the belly of our soul with the corruptible things of this world but rather satisfy it with the word of God. So David, speaking in the person of Adam, fittingly says, "My soul is brought low to the dust; my belly cleaves to the earth." It cleaves to the earth because it is being conformed to the serpent, which feeds on earthly wickedness. And so the Apostle says that we must be conformed to Christ, so that the power of Christ may be displayed in us. This sentence against the serpent should not be thought harsh, since even Adam, whose sin was lighter, is condemned with a similar sentence.

For it is written: "Cursed is the earth in your works; in sorrow you shall eat of it all the days of your life." There certainly seems to be some likeness between the two sentences, yet within that very likeness there is a great difference. It matters whether someone eats earth as was said to the serpent, "it shall eat earth," or as was said to the man, "in sorrow you shall eat." The added words "in sorrow" make the difference, and you should consider how much force that difference has. It is better for me to eat earth in sorrow than in pleasure. That is, in some bodily act and sensation, it is better that I should seem to grieve than to delight in sin; for many, because of their excessive wickedness, do not even become aware of their sin. But he who says, "I chastise my body and bring it into subjection," grieves in repentance for our sins, since his own offenses were not so great that he needed to grieve over them. He also persuades us that this sorrow is useful, the sorrow that is according to God and not according to the world: "You must be grieved," he says, "unto repentance according to God; for sorrow according to God works salvation, but the sorrow of the world works death." You can also learn from the Old Testament that those who grieved over bodily labors attained grace, while those who delighted in such labors remained under punishment. The Hebrews groaned in their labors in Egypt and obtained the grace of the just, and because they ate their bread in sorrow, they were given spiritual food. But the Egyptians, who carried out such works with rejoicing in the service of a detestable king, obtained no pardon.

There is also this distinction: to the serpent it is said that it will eat earth, but to Adam, "In sorrow you shall eat the grass of the field." From this we may understand a kind of progression. When we eat earth, we seem to be in a state of wickedness; when we eat grass, we are making progress; and when we eat bread, our strength has been brought to completion. So let us too make progress in this life, as Paul did. He says, "It is no longer I who live." That is, it is not I who used to eat earth, nor I who ate grass, for "all flesh is grass." "But Christ lives in me": that is, the living bread that came down from heaven lives in me. Wisdom lives, grace lives, justice lives, the resurrection lives.

Next, consider that it is not the man who is cursed but the serpent. Nor is the earth cursed in itself. He says "cursed in your works," and this was said to the soul. The earth is cursed if you have earthly works, that is, worldly works. Even then it is not cursed altogether: it produces thorns and thistles unless it is worked by human effort and labor. But if we work it, we shall eat bread, in labor and sweat indeed, but bread nonetheless. For the law of the flesh fights against the law of the mind, and we must labor and sweat to chastise the body, bring it into subjection, and sow the things that are spiritual. For if we sow the things of the flesh, we shall reap the things of the flesh; but if we sow the things of the spirit, we shall reap the things of the spirit.
